## What it actually was

Not a state, not quite a league either. A loose association of merchant towns, at its height maybe 70 to 200 depending on who you count, with Lübeck as the unofficial head. Philippe Dollinger, *The German Hansa* (Macmillan, 1970), p. 112, is the line I underlined: the Hansa "never had a constitution, a treasury or a permanent army". It worked because merchants trusted each other's courts and boycotts, not because anyone could compel them.

## The four Kontore

The big foreign offices, which I make students learn as a set:

- Bergen: Bryggen, the wooden wharf, stockfish from Lofoten traded for grain.
- London: the Steelyard (Stalhof) on the Thames, closed by Elizabeth I in 1598.
- Bruges: less a compound than a privileged community in the town.
- Novgorod: the Peterhof, furs and wax, the most closed-off of the four.

There was never a Kontor in Ireland. Dublin's trade went to Bristol and Chester. The students are oddly disappointed by this.

## The cog

The standard cargo ship of the Hanse was the cog: flat bottom, high sides, one mast, a stern rudder. The Bremen cog, found in the Weser in 1962 and dated to about 1380, is in the German Maritime Museum in Bremerhaven. Roughly 23 m long, could carry around 90 tonnes. Students like that it was found during dredging, by accident.

## Treaty of Stralsund, 1370

The high point. After war with Valdemar IV of Denmark, the towns got free trade through the Sound, control of several Scania fortresses for 15 years, and a say in the Danish succession. Merchants dictating terms to a king. This is the date I put on the board.

## Decline

- Dutch competition in the Baltic from the 1400s.
- Territorial princes getting stronger and reining in their towns.
- The herring moving away from Scania (overstated in old books, but it's in every textbook).
- The last Hansetag in 1669, attended by just 9 towns. Lübeck, Hamburg and Bremen kept calling themselves Hanseatic cities right up to now; you still see HL and HH on number plates.

## Lübeck, October 2024

Midterm trip, 18 to 21 Oct 2024, flew to Hamburg and took the regional train. The Europäisches Hansemuseum was €16.50 and worth every cent: they rebuilt a corner of the Novgorod Peterhof and a Bruges street. I spent 40 minutes in the room on the 1418 Hansetag. Also: the Holstentor leans, and the marzipan at Niederegger is as good as everyone says.

Saw the Salzspeicher, the salt warehouses beside the Trave. Salt from Lüneburg came up the Stecknitz canal (opened 1398) to Lübeck and on to the Baltic herring trade.

## Overlap with other notes

The Hanse ports moved disease as well as goods: the plague reached Bergen in 1349 on a ship from England ([[Black Death]]). And it makes a nice contrast with [[Roman roads]], where the state built the network; here merchants did it themselves. If I go back to northern Germany it will be with the [[Rail pass Europe]] idea.

## For class

Second years, 3 lessons. Lesson 2 is a role play: each group is a Hanse town deciding whether to join a boycott of Bruges (the real one was 1358). Last time Visby voted against and got "expelled". Good fun, loud.
